newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Civilians quit Zaire rebel areas despite assurances.
newsitem.headline: Civilians quit Zaire rebel areas despite assurances.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila urged civilians on Thursday to stay in rebel-held areas but his words failed to stem the stream of frightened people leaving the eastern city of Goma.
In a speech on rebel Star Radio, Kabila said his forces could defeat any Zairean army counter-attack launched by newly-returned President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"We want to assure you that your security remains absolutely and irreversibly guaranteed," said Kabila, president of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire.

"We are in this liberated territory from Fizi (in the south) to Beni (in the north) and we are here to stay....Mr 'fantastic' Mobutu might attempt to recapture his lost lands, but he is dreaming and he has no idea of our determination," Kabila said.
Despite Kabila's appeal, some residents continued to flee Goma on Thursday and others said they were worried they would be killed in fresh fighting and both sides should now negotiate.

"Kabila might say he is going to protect us, but his past record isn't very good," Jean-Marie Akimungu told Reuters. "Mobutu came back two days ago and it is not clear Kabila has the power to resist him and it is that which makes us afraid."
Hundreds of Goma residents have fled this week, saying they feared for their lives if the army attacked and they doubted the rebels could defend the city they seized in early November.
In his first act since returning from four months in Europe for cancer treatment Mobutu named a new army chief of staff on Wednesday, bringing back a commander tested on the battlefield.
State television said the appointment of General Mahele Bokoungo Lieko was intended to help Zaire's demoralised army meet the challenge of the Tutsi-led revolt in the east.

A close friend of Mobutu, who asked to remain anonymous, said military hardware, including 15 helicopters and several fighter jets, had been brought into Zaire in the past three weeks, accompanied by 154 foreign military personnel.
The Rwandan-backed rebels have seized a swathe of territory 500-km (300-miles) long from north to south since October. Zairean troops, looting as they fled, put up little resistance.
Civilians said the rebellion ended the tyranny of the Zairean army but doubted the rebels could reach as far as the capital Kinshasa.
Residents said they were sending families to Butembo, 200 km (125 miles) north and by bus or boat to Bukavu 150 km (94 miles) south in the hope these towns would escape renewed fighting.
Soldiers said they were screening buses leaving Sake 27 km (16 miles) west of Goma and sending back people trying to flee.
"I believe it is also important to tell you Walikale fell two days ago," Kabila said. Aid workers however said the town, 130-km (80-miles) west of Goma, remained in government hands.
More than 600,000 Rwandan refugees returned to Rwanda from the east during the rebellion but many others fled deeper into eastern Zaire and aid agencies are struggling to reach them.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said on Thursday for the first time it flew food into eastern Zaire beyond rebel lines aboard a Boeing 707 in flights to Kisangani city on Wednesday.
WFP planned to use trucks or small planes to take the 78 tonnes of food to the Lubutu area to the south and sent in three foreign staff to assess the situation in Lubutu and Walikale.
U.N. officials said on Tuesday they had reports of fighting on the outskirts of Walikale and between 50,000 and 100,000 refugees were at Tingi-Tingi seven km (four miles) from Lubutu.
